math_verification: All problem answers hand-verified in problem_spec.verification.

design_principles.principle: One ratio first, the zoo second
design_principles.app_approach: Students master gross profitability — a fraction a twelve-year-old can compute — before meeting Graham's seven criteria and the spanning tests that crown it.
A ψ slider physically flattens the security market line, making Frazzini–Pedersen's funding-constraint theory a thing you operate, with alpha = ψ(1−β) as the payoff formula.
The course's most famous investor becomes a six-factor decomposition students can audit: 12.1% alpha in, 6.3% (insignificant) out.

blocks.block_title: Profitability: The Other Side of Value

slides.title: Pay Up — But Not Too Much
slides.content_summary: Quality has no single definition (profitable, safe, well-run, high payout…); buying quality without paying premium prices IS value investing (Buffett: wonderful business at a fair price). Key structural fact: quality strategies are short value and value strategies short quality — a natural hedge. Two questions: standalone premium, or value enhancer? Stakes: market efficiency.

slides.title: One Ratio: Gross Profits over Assets
slides.content_summary: GP/A = (revenues − COGS)/assets. Sorts: high−low 0.31%/mo (t 2.49) but FF3 alpha 0.52 (t 4.49) — profitable firms are growth-like, so risk adjustment RAISES the anomaly. FM slope 0.75 (t 5.49), industry-demeaned 1.00 (t 8.99); survives earnings and FCF. The economic argument works for risk AND behavioral stories.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Why does the ALPHA exceed the raw spread here, when for momentum the same thing happened for the same reason?'

slides.title: Each Hides the Other
slides.content_summary: Double sorts: conditional profitability spread 58bp vs 31 unconditional; conditional value 68 vs 41 — controlling for each widens the other. Joint 50/50 roughly doubles the Sharpe (0.65–0.78 vs market 0.41) with shallow drawdowns; trailing Sharpes negatively related (value insurance). The measure zoo (Graham's 7, Greenblatt ROIC+EBIT/EV, accruals, Piotroski, defensive): only gross profitability stands alone and survives spanning (alphas 2.34–4.62%/yr); PMU absorbs ROE/market-power/default/net-issuance/org-capital anomalies.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Value and profitability are negatively correlated. Why does that make the COMBINATION stronger, not weaker?'

problem_spec.scenario: Firm A: revenues $100m, COGS $60m, assets $200m. Firm B: revenues $150m, COGS $135m, assets $100m.
problem_spec.verification: GP/A_A = (100−60)/200 = 40/200 = 0.20. GP/A_B = (150−135)/100 = 15/100 = 0.15. A is higher quality despite lower revenue — productivity per asset dollar is what the measure prices.

slides.title: The Anomaly Fischer Black Couldn't Sell
slides.content_summary: 1969: Black finds low-beta stocks beat the CAPM at Wells Fargo; the bank refuses to trade it. Theory: investors who can't lever overweight high-beta assets, so E[r] = rf + ψ + βλ with λ = E[rM]−rf−ψ: intercept up, slope down, CAPM-alpha = ψ(1−β). Evidence: flat SML in US stocks 1926–2010 AND bonds 1952–2010.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'If you can\'t borrow, how do you reach for return? And what does that crowd of reachers do to high-beta prices?'

slides.title: Bet Against Beta, Everywhere
slides.content_summary: US-stock BAB Sharpe 0.75 vs HML 0.39, UMD 0.50, SMB 0.25; alphas decline in beta across every asset class tested. Embedded leverage: options and leveraged ETFs earn negative returns per unit exposure — constrained investors pay for built-in leverage. Prop 3: BAB loses when TED spikes (deleveraging). Prop 5: mutual funds and individuals hold high beta; Berkshire and LBO funds buy low beta and lever.

slides.title: Your Turn: Price a Stock When Leverage Is Scarce

problem_spec.scenario: Funding-liquidity CAPM: E[r] = rf + ψ + β·λ with λ = E[rM] − rf − ψ. Take rf = 2%, ψ = 1.5%, E[rM] − rf = 6%. Consider a low-beta stock with β = 0.5.
problem_spec.verification: λ = 6 − 1.5 = 4.5%. Funding-CAPM E[r] = 2 + 1.5 + 0.5×4.5 = 5.75%. Standard CAPM predicts 2 + 0.5×6 = 5.0%. CAPM-alpha = 5.75 − 5.0 = +0.75% = ψ(1−β) = 1.5×0.5. Symmetric check: β=1.5 gives alpha −0.75% — high beta is low alpha.

slides.title: Price Quality, Then Ask Why It's Cheap
slides.content_summary: Cochrane's challenge: explain prices. Gordon rewrite: P/B = profitability×payout/(required return − growth) — the four QMJ components (Profitability, Growth, Safety, Payout), combined as rank z-scores. The price of quality is positive and significant — but R² is only 0.05–0.31. Three hypotheses for the low R²: better measures / hidden risk / underreaction — each with a testable return implication.

slides.title: Quality Pays — and Hedges
slides.content_summary: Decile returns and alphas rise nearly monotonically: US H−L 0.47%/mo (t 2.80), 4F alpha 0.97 (t 8.55), H−L beta −0.38; QMJ factor 4F alpha 0.66 (t 10.2) US, 0.45 (t 5.5) global, with NEGATIVE market/size/value loadings; IR positive in all countries but one; flight-to-quality (negative convex vs market). Analysts price quality — but not enough: implied E[r] falls with quality while realized rises. Verdict: hypothesis (c), underreaction; Graham–Dodd over efficiency, joint hypothesis noted.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'QMJ has negative loadings on MKT, SMB, and HML, and it GAINS in crashes. Why does AFP say any theory of size and value can get into trouble here?'

slides.title: Your Turn: The Gordon Price of Quality

problem_spec.scenario: QMJ's identity: P/B = profitability × payout / (required return − growth). Firm X: profitability 0.30, payout 0.5, required return 10%, growth 5%. Firm Y trades at P/B = 2 with profitability×payout = 0.15 and growth 5%.
problem_spec.verification: X: P/B = (0.30×0.5)/(0.10−0.05) = 0.15/0.05 = 3.0. Y: r = g + prof·payout/(P/B) = 0.05 + 0.15/2 = 0.125 ⟹ 12.5%. Identical quality, different price ⟹ Y's implied required return is higher — quality at a discount is exactly what QMJ buys.

slides.title: Decomposing Buffett
slides.content_summary: Frazzini–Kabiller–Pedersen split Berkshire into public (13F) and private (inferred) books; leverage L = (TA−Cash)/Equity. Six-factor regression: positive MKT and HML, negative SMB; add BAB (0.29, t 2.67) and QMJ (0.43, t 2.34) and the alpha falls from 12.1% (t 3.19) to 6.3% (t 1.58) — statistically indistinguishable from zero. A systematic leveraged cheap-safe-quality portfolio tracks Berkshire's public book.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Does alpha falling to insignificance diminish Buffett — or is identifying BAB+QMJ fifty years early the achievement?'

slides.title: Your Turn: How Much of Buffett Is Factors?

problem_spec.scenario: Berkshire's annualized alpha is 12.1% under the four-factor model. Adding BAB and QMJ reduces it to 6.3%.
problem_spec.verification: Absorbed by BAB+QMJ = 12.1 − 6.3 = 5.8 points. Share = 5.8/12.1 = 47.9%. Nearly half the legend is systematic exposure to cheap, safe, quality stocks — implementable, in principle, by anyone. The remaining 6.3% carries t = 1.58: not statistically distinguishable from zero.

slides.title: The Defensive Verdict
slides.content_summary: Synthesis: profitability hedges value and subsumes rival quality signals; BAB flattens the SML through leverage constraints, pervasive and tied to funding tightness; QMJ earns large alpha with negative risk loadings and flight-to-quality behavior. Together they recover the size effect, explain a swath of anomalies, and decompose Buffett. The lean: constraints + behavior — Graham–Dodd, formalized. Course thread: but with hundreds of published factors, how do we know THESE are real? Lecture 7.
